questions.stem: Fog. Fine on your starboard bow you hear one prolonged blast, repeated about every 2 minutes. What is it, and what do you do?
options: A vessel at anchor; carry on at your present speed
Power-driven making way; slow right down, extreme caution
A vessel in distress; turn towards it at full speed
A sailing vessel; she must keep clear of you
questions.explanation: One prolonged at intervals of not more than 2 minutes is a power-driven vessel making way (Rule 35). It is ahead of your beam, so unless you have determined there is no risk of collision, Rule 19 requires you to reduce to the minimum speed at which you can keep your course, take all way off if necessary, and navigate with extreme caution. A sailing vessel sounds one prolonged, two short, and the steering rules for vessels in sight do not apply in fog.

questions.stem: Fog. Ahead you hear two prolonged blasts about 2 seconds apart, repeated about every 2 minutes. What is it?
options: Two power-driven vessels making way
A vessel aground in the fog
A power-driven vessel stopped, no way on
A vessel intending to overtake you
questions.explanation: Two prolonged blasts about 2 seconds apart is the Rule 35 signal of one power-driven vessel underway but stopped. It is not two vessels. A vessel aground uses the bell with extra strokes, and overtaking signals (two prolonged followed by short blasts) are for vessels in sight in a narrow channel.

questions.stem: Fog. Off your port bow you hear one prolonged followed by two short blasts, about every 2 minutes. What can you conclude?
options: It is definitely a sailing vessel
It is a power-driven vessel altering to port
It is a pilot vessel on station
NUC, RAM, CBD, sail, fishing or towing
questions.explanation: One prolonged, two short is shared by several kinds of vessel under Rule 35, so you cannot tell which from the sound alone. Treat her as a vessel that may not be able to get out of your way. It is not a manoeuvring signal, since those are only used in sight, and the pilot identity signal is four short.

questions.stem: Fog. You hear one prolonged, two short, and straight after it, from a slightly different direction, one prolonged, three short. What is it, and what is the main hazard?
options: Tug and manned tow; don't pass between
Two fishing vessels with nets in the water
A vessel aground and her tender
A sailing vessel tacking
questions.explanation: A towing vessel sounds one prolonged, two short. A manned vessel being towed sounds one prolonged, three short, if practicable straight after the tug. Together they mean a tow, with a towline you cannot see. Never try to cross between the two signals.

questions.stem: Fog in an anchorage. You hear a bell rung rapidly for about 5 seconds, then again about a minute later. What is it?
options: A vessel making way
A vessel at anchor
A vessel in distress
A vessel being towed
questions.explanation: A bell rung rapidly for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute is a vessel at anchor (Rule 35). A vessel making way uses her whistle, and a distress signal would be a continuous sounding, not a regular 5-second burst. Even an anchored vessel is a hazard: keep a careful watch and slow down. A manned tow sounds one prolonged, three short on a whistle.

questions.stem: Fog near a deep-sea anchorage. You hear a bell rung rapidly for about 5 seconds, followed immediately by a gong for about 5 seconds from a point some distance away. What is it?
options: Two small vessels at anchor close together
A vessel aground in the fog
100 m+ at anchor, bell fwd, gong aft
A tug and tow at anchor
questions.explanation: A vessel of 100 m or more at anchor rings the bell in the fore part and immediately afterwards sounds the gong in the after part. The gap between the two sounds hints at her length. The aground signal adds three separate bell strokes before and after the ringing.

questions.stem: Fog. You hear three separate, distinct bell strokes, then rapid ringing for about 5 seconds, then three more separate strokes. What is it, and what does it suggest about your surroundings?
options: A vessel at anchor in deep water
A fishing vessel hauling nets
A distress signal
Aground: shoal water near; check position
questions.explanation: Three strokes before and after the rapid ringing is the aground signal. If she is aground, there is shoal water near her, and possibly near you. Fix your position and slow down. A plain anchor bell has no extra strokes, and continuous sounding is the distress signal.

questions.stem: Fog. You have been hearing an anchor bell ahead. Now, from the same direction, you hear one short, one prolonged, one short on a whistle. What is happening?
options: She is warning you; slow or stop and alter
The anchored vessel is getting underway
The anchored vessel is in distress
The anchored vessel agrees to let you pass
questions.explanation: An anchored vessel may sound one short, one prolonged, one short to warn an approaching vessel of her position and the risk of collision. You are probably closing her. Take way off and open the distance. It is not the agreement signal (prolonged, short, prolonged, short) or a distress signal.

questions.stem: Fog off a pilot boarding station. You hear two prolonged blasts, then four short blasts. What is it?
options: A power-driven vessel stopped, and a separate vessel in doubt
Pilot vessel on duty, stopped, giving her ID signal
A vessel overtaking you on your port side
A vessel aground near the station
questions.explanation: Two prolonged is a power-driven vessel stopped and making no way. A pilot vessel on pilotage duty may add four short as an identity signal. The doubt signal is at least five short, and the overtaking signal is two prolonged followed by one or two short, used only in sight in a narrow channel.

questions.stem: Clear day, narrow channel. A vessel close astern sounds two prolonged, two short. What does she want, and how do you answer if it is safe?
options: She is altering to port; no answer is needed
She intends to overtake you on your starboard side; answer one short
To pass on your port side; answer long-short-long-short
She is in doubt; answer with five short
questions.explanation: Two prolonged, two short means "I intend to overtake you on your port side". If you agree, sound one prolonged, one short, one prolonged, one short, and act to allow safe passing. Two prolonged, one short would be the starboard side. If you are not happy, sound the doubt signal instead.

questions.stem: Clear day. A vessel approaching you, in sight, sounds six short and rapid blasts. What is she telling you, and what should you do?
options: She is in distress; go alongside her
She is altering course to starboard six times
She is a pilot vessel giving her identity
She doubts your action: make it clear, slow or stop
questions.explanation: At least five short and rapid blasts is the Rule 34 doubt signal, so six counts. She is not sure what you are doing. Make your intentions clear with a bold, early action, and slow or stop if needed. It is not a distress signal, and the pilot identity signal is four short in fog.

questions.stem: You are approaching a blind bend in a narrow BC pass. From beyond the point you hear one prolonged blast. What do you do?
options: Answer with one prolonged; go with care
Sound two short to show you will alter to port
Ignore it unless it is foggy
Sound continuous blasts until you see her
questions.explanation: One prolonged at a bend is the Rule 34 bend signal, and an approaching vessel that hears it answers with one prolonged. It applies in any visibility. Two short is a manoeuvring signal for vessels in sight, and a continuous sounding is a distress signal.

questions.stem: Clear weather in a BC harbour. A power-driven vessel at a wharf ahead of you sounds one prolonged blast. What is the most likely meaning?
options: She is making way in fog
She is leaving her berth
She is in distress at the wharf
She intends to overtake you
questions.explanation: In the Canadian waters of a roadstead, harbour, river, lake or inland waterway, a power-driven vessel leaving a dock or berth sounds one prolonged blast. In clear weather it is not a fog signal, and it is not a distress or overtaking signal. Expect her to back or move out into the fairway.

questions.stem: A ferry in sight, about to manoeuvre near you, sounds one short blast. What does it mean?
options: I am altering my course to port
I am operating astern propulsion
I am altering course to starboard
I am leaving the berth now
questions.explanation: One short means "I am altering my course to starboard" under Rule 34(a). Two short is port and three short is astern propulsion. Leaving a berth in a Canadian harbour is one prolonged.

questions.stem: Fog. From a small boat somewhere ahead you hear a horn sounding three short, three prolonged, three short, over and over. What is it?
options: A vessel being towed astern
Three vessels at anchor together
A vessel overtaking another
SOS in Morse: distress
questions.explanation: Three short, three long, three short is SOS, which Annex IV lists as a distress signal by any signalling method, including sound. A towed vessel sounds one prolonged, three short. Treat it as distress: note the bearing and time, slow down, and tell the master.

questions.stem: A power-driven vessel stopped in fog sounds two prolonged blasts with about 2 seconds between them. About how long does the whole signal take, from the start of the first blast to the end of the second?
options: About 10 to 14 seconds
About 4 to 6 seconds
About 20 to 24 seconds
About 2 minutes
questions.explanation: Each prolonged blast lasts 4 to 6 seconds and the gap is about 2 seconds: 4 + 2 + 4 = 10 seconds at the shortest and 6 + 2 + 6 = 14 seconds at the longest. 4 to 6 seconds is a single prolonged blast, and 2 minutes is the maximum interval between signals, not the length of one.
